## Port forwarding done right {#sec-port-forwarding}

### Risks

- Bots scan the entire internet nonstop, so a new open port gets found within hours
- Unpatched software becomes an entry point into your home network
- Weak or default passwords get brute-forced
- Your home IP becomes public, and game servers in particular attract DDoS attempts
- A compromised server can reach every other device in the house

### Mitigations

- Forward only the exact port you need, and never use the router's DMZ setting
- Turn off UPnP so apps can't open ports on their own
- Keep the OS and the app updated
- Strong unique passwords, two-factor where offered, and whitelists for game servers
- Run services in containers as a non-root user
- A firewall on the server (ufw) that allows only the forwarded port
- Put exposed services on a separate VLAN or guest network if your router supports it
- Fail2ban or CrowdSec to block repeated login attempts
- Close the port when you're not using it

### Verify your security posture

- Review the router's forwarding list and confirm UPnP is off
- Scan your public IP from outside: an online port checker, or nmap from a phone on cellular data
- Look up your IP on Shodan to see what the internet sees
- Check what the server is listening on with `ss -tulpn`
- Read the logs for failed logins and unknown connections
- Repeat this checklist after every change, and on a regular schedule

::: {.callout-warning}
## Break it on purpose
Open a port, scan it from outside, and watch bots show up in the logs. Then close it and confirm the scan comes back closed.
:::
